reels.title: The genius in the locked room

beats.say: Could a brilliant person locked in a room with only a notepad fix your broken report?

show.text: Brilliant, but locked in a room
show.sub: Only a notepad and a pen

beats.say: That is a language model. It reads text and writes text. Nothing else. It cannot open a file, run a query, or remember yesterday.

show.title: A model only reads and writes *text*

chip.text: No files, no queries, no memory

beats.say: Now add an assistant outside the door. You slip a note out saying, check the sales table. The assistant does it and slides the answer back.
That assistant is the harness, ordinary code around the model. Agent equals model plus harness. A weak one wastes money and invents facts. A good one gets real work done.

show.sub: The harness decides how useful the model becomes

check.q: On its own, what can a language model do?
opts: Read text and write text only
Run queries and remember past chats
Open files and call APIs directly
check.why: The model only turns text into text. Running tools and keeping memory are done by the harness, the code around it.

work: Write down which jobs in your team are done by the model and which by your own code.
Next time an AI tool gives a wrong answer, ask whether the model or the harness around it was at fault.

reels.title: The loop inside an agent

beats.say: What actually happens when an agent fixes a failed pipeline?
The harness sends the task and a list of tools to the model. The model replies with a request, like run this query. The model runs nothing itself.
The harness runs the tool and sends the result back. The model reads it and picks the next step. This repeats until it says done, or hits a limit, say twenty turns.
Each turn costs time and tokens. If you already know the steps, call A then B then C. That is a workflow, and it is cheaper. Use a loop only when steps cannot be known in advance.

show.title: Workflow or agent?
items: Workflow: fixed steps you design, A then B then C
Agent: model picks the next step in a loop
Every loop turn costs time and tokens

check.q: When should you choose an agent over a workflow?
opts: Whenever the task uses a language model
When the steps cannot be known in advance
When you want the lowest cost per run
check.why: A workflow is cheaper and more predictable. An agent is worth its loop cost only when the path depends on what it finds along the way.

work: List your current AI jobs and mark each as fixed steps or open-ended.
Set a maximum turn count on every agent loop you run.

reels.title: Where agent loops break

beats.say: Why can a ten step agent cost far more than ten times one call?

show.text: Ten steps, more than ten times the cost?

beats.say: Because the model remembers nothing. On every turn the harness resends the whole conversation. Turn one sends a thousand tokens. Turn ten may send ten thousand, including every tool result.

Failure modes live in the harness. An agent can repeat the same failing query forever, so you cap turns and budget. It can invent a table name, so you validate tool inputs. It can drop a table, so you give read-only access.

show.title: Guards the harness must enforce
items: Loop forever: cap turns and spend

beats.say: And log every step, so you can replay exactly what happened.

check.q: An agent keeps retrying the same failing query. Which fix belongs in the harness?
opts: Ask the model to try harder
A turn cap and spend budget with a stop
Use a bigger model
check.why: The model cannot be trusted to stop itself. The harness enforces hard limits so a bad loop ends cheaply.

work: Add a turn cap, token budget and timeout to every agent run.
Give agent database credentials read-only unless a human approves a write.
Store each tool call and result so a run can be replayed.

reels.title: Agent or workflow: choose with cost in mind

beats.say: Should this pipeline fix be an agent or a workflow?
Default to a workflow. It is predictable, testable, and costs a fixed number of calls. A nightly job with three known steps never needs a loop deciding what to do.
Choose an agent when the path is unknown, like diagnosing why a table is stale, where causes vary every time. You pay with variable cost, slower runs, and harder testing.
Often the best design is a hybrid. A workflow wraps one small agent step, with turn limits, a budget, and a human approval before any write.

check.q: A nightly job always runs the same three steps. What should you build?
opts: An agent, so it can adapt
A workflow with fixed steps
Two agents that review each other
check.why: Known steps need no decision loop. A workflow gives fixed cost and predictable behavior.

work: Review each agent you run and ask whether a fixed workflow could do the same job.
Where you keep an agent, wrap it in a workflow with a budget and approval for writes.
Track cost per run so you can see when a loop is not paying for itself.

reels.title: The agent loop as a locked room

beats.say: How does an AI finish a job when nobody told it the steps? It runs one simple loop, again and again.
Picture a manager locked in a room with a notepad. She cannot leave. She writes a note: please check the sales number. A runner reads it, goes and checks, and slides the answer under the door.
She reads the answer, then writes the next note. Think, act, look at the result. Round and round.
When she finally writes a final answer instead of a note, the runner stops. And the runner can refuse any dangerous note.

check.q: In the locked room story, who actually goes out and does things in the real world?
opts: The manager writing notes
The runner
Both of them equally
check.why: The model only writes requests. Your code, the runner, does the real work, which is why you can refuse or check a request first.

work: Explain the think, act, observe loop to a non-technical colleague using the runner story.
Name one action in your own system that a runner should refuse without approval.

reels.title: The loop in ten lines

beats.say: What is an agent, really? A list of messages and a while loop.

show.title: The whole agent

beats.say: Start with a list holding the task. Send it to the model with the tools it may use. It replies with either plain text, or a request such as: tool run sql, query count orders.
If it asked for a tool, your code runs it and appends the request and the output to the list. That is think, act, observe.
Say a task needs six queries. That is seven model calls: six tool requests and one final answer. Each call resends the whole growing list, so cost climbs every step.
No tool request means done. Return the text.

check.q: A task needs six tool calls before the answer. How many model calls happen?
opts: Six
Seven
One
check.why: Each tool request is one model call, and the final text answer is one more, so seven.

work: Write the loop from memory in your language of choice.
Log the token count sent on each step of one real run to see the growth.

reels.title: Stop conditions and gotchas

beats.say: What stops a confused agent? Nothing, unless you build it in.
Done: the model answers without asking for a tool. Budget: cap the steps, say at twenty five, and cap tokens or dollars. Without a cap, a confused agent loops all night and you pay for it.

show.title: Two easy stops
items: Budget: step cap and money cap

beats.say: No progress: the same tool with the same input twice in a row, or the same error three times. Retrying blindly will not help, because the model sees the same situation. Stop and report what happened.
Remember, the model only asks. So before running, your code can refuse, sandbox it, or ask a human to approve a risky delete.

check.q: An agent gets the same database permission error three times. What should the loop do?
opts: Retry with a longer timeout
Stop and report the repeated error
Raise the step limit
check.why: Repeating the same failure shows no progress. Stop and report instead of burning budget on blind retries.

work: Add a step limit and a cost limit to every agent loop you run.
Track the last tool call and input, and abort on an exact repeat.
Put an approval gate in front of any write or delete tool.

reels.title: When a loop is the wrong tool

beats.say: Should every problem get an agent loop? Usually no.
A loop costs more because every step resends the full history, so cost grows faster than the step count. It is also slower and less predictable.
If you know the steps in advance, write a fixed pipeline. It is cheaper, easy to test, and takes the same path every time. Use a loop only when the next step depends on what the last one found.

When you do loop, keep control outside the model: budgets, approval gates for writes, and logs of every request. Add a judge, like running tests, and feed its verdict back. That is how loops improve themselves.

check.q: Which task best justifies an agent loop over a fixed pipeline?
opts: Nightly copy of one table with the same steps
Debugging a failing job where each finding decides the next check
Sending a daily report from a template
check.why: A loop earns its cost when the next step depends on what the last step found. Fixed, known steps are cheaper and more predictable as a pipeline.

work: Review your agents and replace any with fixed steps by a plain pipeline.
Set per-run budgets and alerts so a runaway loop is caught early.
Add a test or reviewer check as the judge for any loop that produces code or data.

reels.title: Fix the kitchen, not the recipe

beats.say: Your new cook burns the toast. Do you rewrite the recipe, or fix the kitchen?

show.text: Rewrite the recipe, or fix the kitchen?

beats.say: Most people reword the instructions they give an AI agent. That is called the prompt. It helps a little, but the agent can still make the same mistake tomorrow.
Harness engineering fixes the kitchen instead. Put a timer on the toaster. Lock the knife drawer. Add a checklist by the door. Now that mistake simply cannot happen.

show.title: Change the environment
items: A lock on the knife drawer

beats.say: A harness is everything around the agent: its tools, its checks, its limits, and a record of what it did. Fix the environment once, and every future run is safer.

check.q: An agent keeps making the same mistake. What is the harness engineering response?
opts: Reword the prompt more firmly
Change the environment so the mistake cannot happen
Switch to a bigger model and hope
Ask the agent to try harder
check.why: Harness engineering changes the surroundings, such as tools, checks and limits, so the mistake becomes impossible rather than merely discouraged.

work: List the last three mistakes your agent made and ask which could be blocked structurally.
Before editing a prompt, ask whether a check or permission could prevent the error instead.

reels.title: The five layers of a harness

beats.say: An agent said it was done, but nothing worked. How do you stop that from happening?

A production harness has five layers. Tools: small, clearly named, with timeouts and retries, so one slow call cannot hang everything. Verification: after every step, run tests, linters and row counts.

Context: give each step only what it needs, and keep a notes file of lessons so old mistakes are not repeated. Guardrails: budgets, read-only roles, sandboxes, and human approval before anything irreversible.
Observability: log every call with its input, output, tokens, cost and time. Without that trace, you cannot tell why a run failed or what it cost.

check.q: Which layer stops an agent from reporting success when nothing actually works?
opts: Observability
Verification
Guardrails
Context and memory
check.why: Verification runs tests, linters, schema checks and row counts after each step, so a claim of done needs evidence.

work: Add a row count or schema check after each write step in your agent pipeline.
Log input, output, tokens, cost and duration for every agent call.

reels.title: Why agents quit early and rush

beats.say: Why does an agent announce success when the job is only half done?
Three known failures. It stops early and declares victory. It rushes when its context window, its working memory, fills up. Or it tries to do too much in one pass and loses track.

show.title: Three failure modes
items: Rushes as the context fills up
Does too much in one pass

beats.say: The fixes are structural. Give it a checklist where each item needs evidence, like a passing test or a row count, before it can be ticked.
Start a fresh context for each sub-task, so memory never fills. And allow one change per iteration, so when something breaks you know which change did it.

check.q: An agent rushes and cuts corners late in a long session. Which fix targets the cause?
opts: Tell it to be careful in the prompt
Give it a fresh context for each sub-task
Increase its retry count
Remove the checklist
check.why: Rushing happens as the context fills up. A fresh context per sub-task removes the cause structurally.

work: Split long agent jobs into sub-tasks that each start with a clean context.
Require a piece of evidence, such as a test result, for every checklist item.
Limit each iteration to a single change so regressions are easy to pin down.

reels.title: Right-sizing the harness

beats.say: Is more harness always better? No. Every layer costs money and speed.

show.text: More harness is not always better

beats.say: Verification adds a test run to every step. Fresh contexts repeat setup tokens. Human approval can stall a pipeline overnight. Tracing every call adds storage and a bill of its own.

show.title: Every layer has a price
items: Verification: a test run per step

beats.say: So scale the harness to the blast radius. A read-only reporting query needs a budget and a trace. A job that drops or rewrites tables needs a sandbox, strict checks, and a human sign-off.

show.title: Match the harness to the *blast radius*

beats.say: And prefer a hard block over a polite prompt. A read-only database role cannot be talked out of anything. Reword the prompt only when no structural fix exists.

check.q: A nightly agent only reads data to build a summary. What is the best-sized harness?
opts: Human approval on every query
A full sandbox plus manual review of each run
A read-only role, a cost budget and a trace
Only a stricter prompt
check.why: Blast radius is small, so cheap hard limits and observability suffice. Heavy approval adds cost without reducing meaningful risk, and a prompt alone enforces nothing.

work: Classify each agent job by what it can damage, then assign guardrails to match.
Replace prompt warnings such as never delete with read-only roles wherever possible.

reels.title: A prompt is a good brief

beats.say: Why does the same AI helper give a brilliant answer one day and nonsense the next? Often, the problem is the brief you wrote.

show.sub: Quality starts with what you ask

beats.say: Imagine hiring a plumber you have never met. If you say only, fix my house, you get a guess. Tell them who they are, the job, what you have already seen, the rules, how to report back, and show a sample.
A good prompt is that brief. It has six labelled parts: role, task, context, constraints, output format and examples. The labels work like folders, so nothing blurs together.
Say what good looks like. Quote the evidence beats be accurate, because you can check whether the helper did it.

show.sub: Quote the proof, not be accurate

check.q: Which instruction gives the AI helper the clearest idea of success?
opts: Be accurate and thorough
Quote the log line that proves the cause
Try your best on this one
check.why: It names something you can check. Adjectives like accurate or thorough cannot be verified; a quoted line either exists or it does not.

work: Rewrite one vague prompt you use so it states what a good answer contains.
Label the parts of a prompt you reuse: role, task, context, rules, format.
Replace one adjective like good or accurate with a checkable requirement.

reels.title: The six parts of a reliable prompt

beats.say: What does a prompt need so an Airflow failure gets diagnosed, not guessed at?

Wrap six parts in tags. Role says who is answering: a data reliability engineer. Task gives one job: explain the failure and propose one fix. Context pastes in the log tail, the DAG code and the last good run.

Constraints set the bar: quote the log line that proves the cause, say so if unsure, and stay under 120 words. Output format asks for JSON with cause, evidence, fix and confidence. One good example shows the shape.

show.title: Output shape
show.text: {cause, evidence, fix, confidence: low | medium | high}

beats.say: Why tags? They let the model tell your instructions apart from the pasted log, so messy log text is less likely to be mistaken for orders.

check.q: Why wrap the pasted log in its own context tag?
opts: It makes the prompt shorter
It helps the model separate your instructions from the data
It forces the answer to be valid JSON
check.why: Tags mark where instructions end and data begins. They do not shorten the prompt or guarantee JSON; that is the job of the output format part.

work: Convert one of your free-text prompts into the six tagged parts.
Put every pasted log or document inside its own context tag.
Add a constraint that demands evidence, such as quoting the exact line.

reels.title: Structured output with one retry

beats.say: Your code expects JSON, but the model replies with a friendly paragraph. What breaks?

Everything downstream. The parser fails at three in the morning and nobody gets the alert. So when code reads the answer, ask for a fixed shape: cause, evidence, fix, and confidence as low, medium or high.
Then validate it. Check every field is present and that confidence is one of the three allowed words.

show.title: Validate
items: Confidence is low, medium or high

beats.say: If validation fails, send the exact error back to the model once. Missing field evidence is a precise hint, and one retry often fixes the slip. Endless retries just burn tokens and money. After that, flag a human.

check.q: A reply fails validation. What is the best next step?
opts: Retry in a loop until it passes
Send the validation error back to the model once
Ignore the field and continue
check.why: The specific error guides a fix. A single retry caps cost; unbounded loops waste money and may never succeed, so escalate after that.

work: Add schema validation between every model call and the code that reads it.
Cap retries at one and log the validation error.
Route repeated failures to a human queue or alert.

reels.title: Think harder only when it pays

beats.say: Is it smart to tell the model to think hard on every prompt?

No. Reasoning means extra tokens written before the answer. Tokens cost money and add seconds of waiting. For diagnosing a failed task or designing a pipeline, that is worth it. For reformatting a date, it is waste.
Second trap: stuffing three jobs into one prompt, like classify, summarise and draft a fix. When the answer is wrong, you cannot tell which job failed.
Split them into steps. Each has its own input and expected output, so you can test and fix one at a time.

check.q: Why split classify, summarise and draft a fix into separate prompts?
opts: Each step can be tested and debugged on its own
It always makes the model cheaper
The model cannot read long prompts
check.why: Separate steps give isolated inputs and expected outputs, so a failure points to one step. Cost may even rise, and length is not the main issue.

work: Mark which prompts need reasoning and turn it off for formatting tasks.
Split any prompt that does more than one job.
Give each step its own expected output so it can be tested.

reels.title: Prompts need tests, and sometimes code

beats.say: You tweaked one sentence in a prompt and it feels better. How do you know you did not break ten other cases?
You do not, without tests. Keep twenty real inputs with expected answers. Score every prompt change against them, like a unit test suite for the prompt.

Know the trade-offs. Twenty cases is a cheap start, not proof, and it misses rare failures. Each run costs tokens, so run the full set on changes, not every keystroke. Grow the set from every production miss.
And ask whether you need a prompt at all. If the answer is deterministic, like parsing a known log pattern, plain code is cheaper, faster and exact.

check.q: A log format never changes and you only need the error code from it. What do you choose?
opts: A long prompt with examples
A reasoning-enabled prompt
A regular expression or parser
check.why: Deterministic extraction is exact, free and fast with code. Prompts add cost, latency and variability where none is needed.

work: Build a 20-case test set for your most important prompt and score changes against it.
Add each production failure to the test set.
Review your prompts and replace any deterministic ones with plain code.

reels.title: The prompt that runs itself

beats.say: Do you ever repeat the same chore every single morning, exactly the same way?
If you type the same prompt to an AI every day, you are doing that chore. Write the steps down once as a script, which is just a small program saved in a folder with history.
Next, add an alarm clock. A scheduler runs the script at seven every morning while you sleep.
Add a smoke alarm too. If the job breaks, it messages you. And the password it uses, called an API key, stays in a locked safe, never taped to the front door.

check.q: Where should the API key for an automated prompt job be kept?
opts: In the script file in git
In the CI secret store
In the prompt text
check.why: Anything committed to git can be read by anyone with repo access and stays in history. The CI secret store hands the key to the job only when it runs.

work: List one prompt you run by hand every week and write down what inputs it needs.
Check that no API keys sit in any repo you own.
Put the prompt and its input-gathering code in one file in git.

reels.title: From hand-run prompt to scheduled job

beats.say: How does a prompt you run by hand become a job that runs itself?
Step one, a script. Code gathers the inputs, say yesterday's failed pipeline runs, drops them into the prompt, and calls the model. It lives in git, so changes are reviewed.
Step two, a schedule. A GitHub Actions workflow with a schedule trigger, or cron, or Airflow, starts it daily at six. Public repos run free, and private ones get a monthly free allowance.

show.title: Pick a scheduler
items: GitHub Actions schedule: free for public repos

beats.say: Step three, write to a dated file, like report dash 2026 dash 11 dash 07, so a rerun overwrites instead of duplicating. Step four, on failure, post to Slack with the trace link.

steps.label: On failure: Slack plus trace link

check.q: Why write the result to a file named with the date?
opts: So the file sorts nicely
So a rerun replaces the same file instead of adding a duplicate
So the model remembers yesterday
check.why: A dated name gives the job a fixed target per day. Running it twice leaves one file, which is what idempotent output means.

work: Add a schedule trigger to one workflow and test it with a manual run first.
Name every output by its run date or upsert on a date key.
Add a Slack webhook step that fires only on failure and includes the trace link.

reels.title: Where automated prompts break

beats.say: Your nightly job failed at three a m, you retry it, and now there are two reports. What went wrong?
The output was not idempotent, meaning running it twice should leave the same result as once. Fix it by writing to a file named for the date, or by upserting a row keyed on that date.
Two more traps. Alerts only fire if the job fails loudly, so a model returning empty or wrong text passes silently. Check the output's shape before saving it.

show.title: Silent failures
items: Empty or wrong text still exits clean
Validate length and format before saving
Fail the job if the check fails

beats.say: And secrets: an API key committed to git stays in history even after you delete it. Keep keys in the CI secret store, and rotate any key that leaked.

check.q: A scheduled prompt job returns an empty string and exits with code zero. What happens with basic failure alerts?
opts: An alert fires
Nothing fires, so you need an output check that fails the job
The scheduler retries automatically
check.why: Failure alerts react to errors or nonzero exits. Bad content that exits cleanly slips through, so validate the output and fail on purpose.

work: Add a check that fails the job on empty or malformed model output.
Test idempotency by running the job twice and counting rows or files.
Scan git history for keys and rotate any that appear.

reels.title: When not to automate a prompt

beats.say: When is automating a prompt a bad idea?
When it runs rarely, or when a wrong answer is costly and no one checks it. Automation turns one mistake into a mistake every day. Build it only after you have fixed the prompt by hand several times.

Pick the lightest scheduler that fits. A GitHub Actions schedule is free and enough for one daily job. Move to Airflow when jobs depend on each other, need backfills, or need retries across many tasks. Actions schedules can start late and have time limits, so avoid it for exact timing.
Finally, review weekly. Look at cost and accuracy, and turn repeated human corrections into prompt or tool changes. That is how the job pays for itself.

check.q: Which case best justifies moving from a GitHub Actions schedule to Airflow?
opts: One prompt runs once a day
Many jobs depend on each other and need backfills and retries
You want the job to be free
check.why: Airflow earns its overhead when you must manage dependencies, backfills and per-task retries. A single daily job is cheaper to run on a simple schedule.

work: Hold a weekly ten-minute review of cost and accuracy for each automated prompt.
Log every manual correction and fold repeats into the prompt or a tool.
Write down the trigger for moving a job off Actions before it gets complex.

reels.title: The AI taxi meter

beats.say: Why can the same question cost ten times more on one day than on another?

Think of a taxi. You pay for the distance you ride, and for the size of the car. An AI model works the same way. You pay for the words you send in, the words it writes back, and how fancy the model is.
So to pay less, ride a shorter distance or take a smaller car. Send fewer words. Ask for shorter answers. Use a cheaper model when the trip is easy.

show.title: Three ways to pay less
items: Use a smaller model for easy trips

check.q: In the taxi picture, which three things decide what you pay?
opts: Words in, words out, and model size
Only the time of day
Only how many users you have
check.why: Cost is input tokens plus output tokens, multiplied by the price of the model you chose.

work: Look at one recent AI task and write down roughly how many words went in and came out.
Ask which parts of that task really needed the biggest model.

reels.title: Nurse or surgeon

beats.say: Would you book a brain surgeon to put on a plaster?

show.sub: Not every job needs the best one

beats.say: A hospital sends easy cases to a nurse and hard cases to a surgeon. Models work the same way. Sorting an email into a folder is easy, so a small cheap model does it. Working out why a pipeline broke is hard, so a large model earns its price.

show.title: Send each job to the right *expert*

chip.text: Most jobs are easy and cheap

beats.say: The rule is simple. Pick the smallest model that still passes your tests. If the nurse gets every case right, you never pay for the surgeon.

check.q: Which job is best sent to a small, cheap model?
opts: Designing a new data platform
Sorting support emails into five labels
Diagnosing a rare outage across many systems
check.why: Classification is a narrow, easy task. Diagnosis and design are hard and justify a large model.

work: List the steps in one workflow and mark each easy or hard.
Try the easy steps on a smaller model and compare the results.

reels.title: Caching: pay once, read cheap

beats.say: What if reading the same page a second time cost one tenth of the first?

That is prompt caching. Say your prompt starts with twenty thousand tokens of tools, rules and documents. The first call writes them to a cache. A five minute write costs one point two five times normal, so twenty five thousand units.
Every later call inside five minutes reads that prefix at one tenth, just two thousand units. After ten calls you pay about forty three thousand, not two hundred thousand.
The catch is that the prefix must match exactly, word for word.

show.sub: One changed word means a miss

check.q: A 20,000 token prefix is cached with a 5 minute write. What do the next calls inside 5 minutes cost for that prefix?
opts: About 25,000 units each
About 2,000 units each
Nothing at all
check.why: A cache read costs about 0.1 times normal input, so 20,000 tokens becomes roughly 2,000 units.

work: Find the longest unchanging part of your biggest prompt.
Work out how many calls you make per 5 minutes to see if a cache write pays back.

reels.title: Send less, write less

beats.say: Your agent answers a question about one customer. Why is it reading fifty thousand rows?
Because someone pasted the whole table. Retrieve the five relevant rows instead, or the last fifty log lines, not the whole log. Input falls from about fifty thousand tokens to about five hundred.

Now the output side. Output tokens usually cost several times more than input. Set max tokens, ask for a short structured answer like a label and a reason, and never ask the model to repeat the input back.

show.title: Cap the output
items: Ask for label plus short reason

beats.say: Fewer tokens in, fewer tokens out, same answer.

check.q: Which change cuts cost most for a question about one customer?
opts: Retrieve only that customer's rows
Add please to the prompt
Ask the model to repeat the table first
check.why: Sending only relevant data shrinks input by orders of magnitude. Repeating input adds expensive output.

work: Replace one full-table or full-log paste with a retrieval step.
Add a max tokens cap and a short answer format to your noisiest prompt.

reels.title: Why the cache never hits

beats.say: You turned on caching, but the bill did not move. What went wrong?

A cache matches an identical prefix, from the very first token. If a timestamp or request ID sits near the top, every call looks new, so the cache never hits. Put stable things first: tools, system prompt, long documents. Put changing things last.

chip.text: Cache breakpoint goes before the changing part

beats.say: Also, the cache expires after five minutes without a hit. Traffic that arrives every ten minutes pays the write price each time, and a write costs more than a normal call.

show.title: Expiry trap
items: Five minute life, refreshed by each hit
Gaps over five minutes mean a new write

beats.say: Prove it works. Read cache read input tokens in the response. If it is zero, you are not saving anything.

check.q: A request ID is placed at the top of the system prompt, before a long document. What happens to caching?
opts: It still hits, since the document is identical
It misses every call, because the prefix differs from the first token
It hits, but costs double
check.why: Caching needs an identical prefix. A changing ID early on makes every prefix unique, so nothing is reused.

work: Move timestamps, IDs and user text to the end of your prompts.
Log cache_read_input_tokens on every call and alert when it is zero.

reels.title: When a cap or a loop bites back

beats.say: You capped output at two hundred tokens and now your JSON will not parse. Why?

Because max tokens is a hard cut, not a hint. The model stops mid sentence, and a half written object is broken. Size the cap above your longest valid answer, and check the stop reason for truncation.

Loops hide bigger waste. An agent that retries forever re-sends its whole growing history each turn, so cost grows faster than the number of turns. Set a turn limit and a budget, and stop when the goal is met.
And log tokens and cost per task, or you are guessing.

show.sub: Tokens and cost per task in the trace

check.q: Why does a long agent loop get expensive faster than the turn count suggests?
opts: Each turn re-sends the growing history as input
The model charges more per turn number
Output is always free in loops
check.why: Every turn includes earlier messages, so total input tokens grow roughly with the square of the turns.

work: Add a max-turns limit and a token budget to every agent loop.
Alert when stop_reason is max_tokens on structured outputs.

reels.title: Cheaper per call, dearer overall

beats.say: A cheaper model saves sixty percent per call. So why can it raise your total bill?

Because the cost that matters is cost per correct result. If the small model fails one task in four, retries and human fixes eat the saving. Build an eval first, then route only the steps where the small model passes.
Batch APIs are discounted but slow, so use them for nightly backfills, never for a user waiting. Caching only pays when the same prefix returns often. For a one-off prompt, skip it.
Track cost per successful task, and optimise the biggest line first.

check.q: A small model is 60 percent cheaper but fails 40 percent of tasks, each needing a large-model retry. What should you do?
opts: Use it everywhere, since each call is cheaper
Measure cost per successful task before routing to it
Remove the eval to save tokens
check.why: Retries and failures can cancel the saving. Compare cost per correct result on an eval before switching.

work: Compute cost per successful task for your top workflow, not just cost per call.
Move one non-urgent job to a batch API and compare the bill.

reels.title: The folder on the desk

beats.say: Imagine hiring a brilliant consultant who forgets everything the moment they leave the room. All they know is the folder on the desk. So what do you put in it?
Only what matters. Stuff in fifty pages and they miss the key line. Leave out your company's own meaning of a phrase like active customer, and they guess. So the folder is small and relevant.
Put the standing rules at the front, the same every visit. Put today's question at the back. Add two or three sample answers so they see the style you want.

show.title: Order the folder
items: Front: standing rules, same every time
Middle: two or three sample answers

beats.say: And when the history gets long, don't hand over every old email. Write a short note: the goal, what is done, and what comes next.

check.q: Why does the consultant analogy say to keep the folder small and relevant?
opts: Because the consultant only knows what is in the folder, and extra noise hides the key facts
Because the consultant remembers last week's meetings anyway
Because longer folders are always rejected
check.why: The model knows only what it sees in the prompt, so noise can bury the facts that matter and missing definitions force guesses.

work: Write down the three facts a newcomer would need to answer your most common question, and check your prompt contains them.
Add a short goal, done, next note to any long-running chat or agent task instead of pasting the whole history.

reels.title: Why prompt order changes your bill

beats.say: Why does the order of your prompt change your bill? Because providers cache from the front of the prompt.

show.sub: Caching works on the front of the prompt

beats.say: Say your instructions, tool descriptions and schema take six thousand tokens, and the question takes fifty. Put the six thousand first. The provider reuses that processed start, and cached tokens cost about a tenth. Change one word at the top and the match breaks, so changing material goes last.
History grows too. Forty turns at five hundred tokens each is twenty thousand tokens, resent on every call. Replace it with a three hundred token state block: goal, done so far, next step.
Then add two or three examples of the output you want, including one edge case, so the model copies the shape instead of guessing it.

check.q: Which prompt layout gives the best chance of cache hits?
opts: Current question first, then instructions and schema
Instructions, tools and schema first, current question last
Schema in the middle, shuffled each call
check.why: Caches match an identical prefix, so stable material must come first and changing material last.

work: Reorder your prompt so instructions, tool descriptions and schema come before the user question.
Measure tokens per call, then replace resent history with a short state block.

reels.title: Why the cache hit rate hit zero

beats.say: Your prompt cache hit rate dropped to zero overnight. Nobody touched the instructions. What happened?

Someone added the current time to the top of the prompt. Cache matching needs an identical prefix, so every call looked new. Put timestamps and user details at the end, and keep tool lists in a fixed order.

Other traps. Long context is not free attention: facts buried in the middle get missed, so place key facts near the start or end. A summary can drop a detail, and the next summary builds on the loss, so keep ids and hard constraints word for word.
Examples pull hard. Show one edge case and the model may produce it everywhere. And sample rows can leak personal data, so mask them first.

show.title: More gotchas
items: Sample rows can leak personal data
Stale schema gives confident wrong SQL

check.q: Cache hits vanish after a release that put the request time at the top of the system prompt. Why?
opts: The model forgot the instructions
The prefix now differs on every call, so nothing matches
Timestamps are blocked by caches
check.why: Caches need an identical prefix. A value that changes each call at the top makes every prefix unique.

work: Audit your prompt for timestamps, ids or user names near the top and move them to the end.
Keep ids, dates and constraints verbatim in summaries, and mask personal data in sample rows.

reels.title: Don't paste the whole warehouse

beats.say: Context windows now hold a million tokens. So why not paste in the whole warehouse?

Because you pay for every token on every call, and accuracy falls as noise rises. With five thousand tables, retrieve the ten relevant ones by description, then send only those with sample rows and definitions.
Put business definitions in one governed semantic layer, not in each prompt. Then active rider means one thing everywhere, and a change ships once.

show.title: One semantic layer
items: Reused by every prompt and tool

beats.say: Choose by trade-off. Stable style across millions of calls may justify fine-tuning instead of long examples. Summaries save cost but risk drift. Decide with evals: measure accuracy and cost per answer as you trim.

show.title: Cost per answer as context grows

check.q: You have five thousand tables and a text-to-SQL assistant. What is the best default?
opts: Paste every table into every prompt
Retrieve the relevant tables, and attach governed definitions and sample rows
Remove all definitions to save tokens
check.why: Retrieval keeps the prompt small and relevant, cuts cost per call, and a semantic layer keeps meanings consistent.

work: Run an eval that compares accuracy and cost per answer with the full schema, retrieved tables and trimmed history.
Move metric definitions such as active rider into one shared semantic layer that prompts pull from.
